channel.title: DFIR Radar
channel.description: Keeping DFIR Intelligence on your Radar. The latest DFIR research from hundreds of sources, ranked by relevance for practitioners.

item.title: Zammad CVE-2026-102489: Session Leak to RCE
item.description:
Zero-day pair in Zammad helpdesk software chained from unauthenticated session cookie theft to RCE, confirmed exploited against DIVD before patches existed. Both CVEs were used in a breach attributed to an agentic AI-powered attacker.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-102489 is a zero-day confirmed exploited in the wild. A single unauthenticated WebSocket request to the /ws endpoint with the payload {"event": "base"} triggers a Ruby NoMethodError. Because sessions/event.rb returns the full error object to the caller, and because [@]clients stores all active connection state including session headers with no per-client filtering, every authenticated user's session cookie is leaked in that one response. No authentication required, no brute force, one packet.
- The exploit chain continues post-cookie-theft via Zammad's package installation endpoint, which accepts arbitrary file writes into the application directory. An attacker with a stolen admin session cookie writes a malicious ERB template that overrides the built-in password reset email view, then triggers a password reset for any account. Zammad's mailer renders the attacker-controlled template with full Ruby execution privileges, achieving RCE as the zammad OS user. The second zero-day, CVE-2026-102490, then escalates that to root and remains unpatched. Horizon3[.]ai is withholding those details.
- DFIR artifact focus: DIVD released an IOC script that parses Zammad error logs for leaked session cookie strings. That log evidence is the forensic fingerprint of exploitation. On a potentially compromised Zammad host, examine application error logs for NoMethodError output containing [@]clients or cookie material, review the package installation endpoint's activity for unexpected file writes, and check the views directory for modified or unfamiliar ERB templates, particularly anything touching password reset email rendering.
- The initial breach victim here was DIVD itself, a vulnerability coordination body. DIVD attributed attacker behavior to agentic AI tooling based on their forensic artifacts, and Horizon3[.]ai independently reproduced the vulnerability discovery using an AI research harness with Anthropic's Opus 4.8 as the model, reaching a working trigger in hours. The attack surface is any internet-exposed Zammad instance running the vulnerable version.
Practitioner takeaway: pull the DIVD IOC script and run it against Zammad error logs immediately. Hunt for POST or GET activity to the /ws WebSocket endpoint, particularly single-request sessions with no subsequent authenticated behavior that nonetheless correlate with new admin activity. Look for file creation events inside the Zammad application directory that postdate any suspicious WebSocket traffic. CVE-2026-102490 has no patch yet, so treat any confirmed CVE-2026-102489 hit as a full-compromise scenario until proven otherwise. Horizon3[.]ai's proof-of-concept is publicly available on their GitHub.

item.title: 100+ Compromised Websites Use Fake Cloudflare Checks to Deliver LunexStealer
item.description:
UAC-0277 is running a 100+ site ClickFix campaign against Ukrainian 🇺🇦 internet users, using fake Cloudflare checks to drop LunexStealer and a malicious browser extension that hijacks browsing sessions and exfiltrates files.
Key details:
- The attack chain is layered: compromised websites are injected with JavaScript that reads operating mode and domain from a Polygon or Ethereum smart contract (EtherHiding), making the C2 infrastructure harder to block at the network layer. Mode 2 targets Windows users arriving from search engines, shows the fake CAPTCHA no more than twice in 12 hours, and prompts them to execute a command via the Run dialog, the ClickFix social engineering technique that drops a malicious MSI.
- Three MSI variants have been identified. Variant 1 installs LunexStealer directly. Variant 2 attempts UAC bypass, adds Microsoft Defender exclusions, and abuses the legitimate but vulnerable AMD driver PDFWKRNL.sys to blind security tooling before fetching and running the stealer from a remote server. Variant 3 uses DLL sideloading: the legitimate binary FnHotkeyUtility.exe loads a rogue DLL spkvol.dll, which decrypts and executes LunexStealer in memory.
- LunexStealer deploys a malicious browser extension called LUNARAXE, masquerading as "Microsoft Office Word Editor." LUNARAXE is modular: LUNARAXE.CORE handles C2 comms and data exfiltration including cookies, credentials, history, and bookmarks, and can manage tabs, run JavaScript on pages, and display fake overlays. LUNARAXE.STEALER captures credentials entered into web forms in real time. LUNARAXE.STRIP disables Content Security Policy protections by stripping CSP headers from HTTP responses to enable arbitrary JavaScript execution. This combination gives the operator persistent, interactive browser control.
- A secondary component, NAIVEMESS, is deployed based on C2 configuration and acts as a PowerShell-based Native Messaging Host bridging LUNARAXE to the Windows file system. It can enumerate drives and directories, read, write, create, and execute files, and transfers data in Base64-encoded chunks with directories pre-archived as ZIP files. NAIVEMESS has no independent C2 channel: all commands route through the extension, meaning standard network-based C2 detections will not catch it in isolation.
- Forensic opportunities are rich. Look for msiexec.exe execution spawned from user-context processes, unexpected writes of PDFWKRNL.sys or spkvol.dll alongside FnHotkeyUtility.exe in non-standard paths, PowerShell processes registered as Native Messaging Hosts under browser configuration directories, and browser extension directories containing unlisted or recently added extensions claiming to be productivity tools. The smart contract C2 means DNS and traditional domain blocklists may miss early-stage traffic; inspect for web3 RPC calls (Polygon or Ethereum endpoints) from browser processes or injected scripts.
Practitioners should prioritize: block the Windows Run dialog for standard users via Group Policy, restrict msiexec.exe to admin contexts and alert on user-context invocations, enable Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist and the ASR rule "Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers" to prevent PDFWKRNL.sys from landing on disk, and enforce a browser extension allowlist. Hunt for FnHotkeyUtility.exe, spkvol.dll, and PDFWKRNL.sys in process and file creation logs. Full IOC list is in the CERT-UA advisory.

item.title: CyberXero: An AI-Augmented Initial Access Broker Targeting Ukrainian Critical Infrastructure
item.description:
A Russian-speaking IAB paired commodity tooling with 51 Claude Code agents and a PentAGI-Cobalt Strike integration to hit Ukrainian 🇺🇦 critical infrastructure at scale. A single exposed open directory broke the whole operation open.
- CyberXero's primary workstation at 46.21.250[.]135 (AS204601, Zomro NL) was left as an open directory with no access control, exposing 90,000+ files across 3,000 subdirectories: engagement folders named after victims, AI agent configs, session logs with plaintext tokens, and exfiltrated database exports. A provisioning token embedded in installation URLs, an internal SSH hostname, and correlated bash histories tied eight distinct nodes together across three ASNs, including a Cobalt Strike Team Server at 42.193.227[.]214 (AS45090, Tencent Cloud) reachable on ports 1002, 8044, and 8033.
- The opportunistic pipeline centers on wp2shell, an internally developed Python package exploiting CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137 in the WordPress REST API batch endpoint to inject SQL, write a rogue admin, and register a WSO-family webshell as an active plugin. The rogue admin username pattern wp2_[0-9a-f]{8} is the sharpest hunt pivot available. A single automated run scanned 4,708 targets, confirmed 429 accessible admin panels, and dropped 32 shells in 61 seconds. CVE-2026-4815 (Support Board 3.8.7, CVSS 8.8) was weaponized within 30 days of disclosure. Persistence arrived via a service named UpdSvc with a binPath pointing to an IEX download from hxxp://42.193.227[.]214:8033/[a-z0-9]{13}.
- The directed pipeline is where this stops looking like a standard IAB. Seven Ukrainian 🇺🇦 energy and utilities entities were under curated manual reconnaissance, including the national transmission system operator and the country's largest private energy holding, with 95 subdomains enumerated covering VPN, email, network dispatch, and data platforms (T1590.002). A hardcoded credential in the actor's own script (T1078.003) gave direct access to a Kharkiv district heating provider; a multithreaded extractor pulled 564,073 subscriber records with home addresses and account numbers plus 213,340 access-log entries. Because Kharkiv sits on an active conflict front, this is a potential physical safety risk to named civilians.
- The AI layer ran in two tiers. On the workstation, 51 specialized Claude Code agents covered roles including c2-operator, exploit-chainer, scada-attacker, lateral-movement, and credential testing. On the Team Server, PentAGI was wired into Cobalt Strike via an AI provider API for payload generation and pentest execution. The actor's own session logs document the evasion techniques used against model refusals: a fictional "authorized pentest on my own infrastructure" narrative appearing verbatim across four unrelated victims (context engineering, not a technical bypass), and session resets to clear refusal state and reload the authorization framing. The logs also record genuine refusals that held across four iterations, declining backdoor installation, firewall disabling, lateral movement, and webshell deployment.
- The WSO webshell (SHA-256: a5ae0aab352871bc0b038b3aa43b03eb223425628c884af7b9fc592cd34eb86c), obfuscated with the R00t-Shell[.]com 2.0.15 obfuscator, was undetected on VirusTotal at analysis time. Additional hashes cover the Cobalt Strike x86 stager (92a789444708fa1cb4cc5a89e0aa6cc7a279b62a7b8a4d2857255a18197d0090) and Chinese 🇨🇳 cluster staging payloads. Redis exploitation nodes at 42.193.100[.]94 used rogue replication (SLAVEOF) to inject SSH public keys into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (T1098.004).
Hunt WordPress admin tables for accounts matching wp2_[0-9a-f]{8} and audit plugin directories for /wp-content/plugins/wp2shell_[0-9a-f]{8}/. Check internet-exposed Redis hosts for unexpected authorized_keys entries. Treat AI agent session logs as credential-tier material: exposed logs are an operational intelligence breach, and session-reset evasion is best controlled through infrastructure-layer logging and auditing, not model-level controls. Full IOC list, YARA rules for the wp2shell artifacts and WSO obfuscated variant, and the complete ATT&CK TTP mapping are in the report.

item.title: Dependency installation security measure already defeated on npm
item.description:
The indexed-btree npm package bypasses npm v12's lifecycle script block by hiding malware inside btree.prototype.set, firing at import time. Audit node_modules for prototype-level loaders and hunt Slack, Telegram, and Ethereum C2 traffic.

item.title: LibreOffice and OpenOffice Flaws Let Malicious Spreadsheets Run Code Without Macro Warnings
item.description:
CVE-2026-59265 leaves Apache OpenOffice 4.1.16 unpatched: a malicious Calc spreadsheet chains a database refresh to remote JAR execution via JDBC silently. Disable Java in OpenOffice settings now; LibreOffice users update to 26.2.5 or 26.8.0.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] StreamSets Transformer 3.17.0 auth-mode none fallback and un-sandboxed ScalaDTransform execution to container root (8.1 primary)
item.description:
StreamSets Transformer 3.17.0 falls open to anonymous Scala code execution as container uid 0 when http.authentication resolves to none. Audit deployed containers for unexpected pipeline definitions and verify effective auth properties.

item.title: Q3 2026 Attack Techniques Trend Report
item.description:
Q3 2026 saw a sharp rise in trusted-path abuse: perimeter exploits, poisoned supply chains, and identity attacks converged as attackers leveraged legitimate infrastructure to persist and expand after initial access.
Key findings:
- CISA KEV added 100 entries between July and September 2026, double the 50 added in Q3 2025. Web and server applications (31) plus network and perimeter devices (30) accounted for 61% of new listings. Notably, 9 development and deployment tools and 6 AI and LLM tools also appeared, signaling that the attack surface is widening beyond classic enterprise targets.
- Perimeter device exploitation was confirmed against NetScaler ADC and Gateway via CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, and against Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center via CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316. Post-exploitation was consistent: threat actors dropped web shells (T1505.003) disguised as .deb filenames or CSS resources on legitimate web paths. In Cisco FMC cases, JSP web shells and JAR command execution executors landed in Tomcat web paths for credential harvesting. Attackers also set SUID and SGID bits on /bin/sh (T1548.001) to enable privilege escalation for follow-on commands.
- Supply chain compromise hit npm and PyPI ecosystems. Malicious versions of the keyv and cacheable packages, plus [@]7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen and MemTensor, were distributed through official registries (T1195). Ten malicious versions of [@]7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen even carried legitimate npm provenance, meaning standard provenance checks would not have caught them. Malware execution paths included preinstall scripts, binding.gyp files, module loading phases, and publication workflow triggers.
- Identity attacks targeted Okta and Microsoft through passkey registration abuse, password recovery flows, and help desk impersonation via calls and SMS (T1566.004). Adversary-in-the-Middle phishing (T1078.004) was used to intercept session tokens, and device code authorization flows were abused to obtain tokens for attacker-controlled clients. Post-access activity spanned OfficeHome, the identity portal, Microsoft Graph, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange, representing full tenant visibility for an attacker.
DFIR takeaway: This quarter's pattern is trusted-path abuse across every layer. For perimeter response, check for new files in /vpn/scripts/linux/ and /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/, audit web server config changes, inspect /bin/sh permissions, and hunt for web shell invocations in web server logs. For supply chain incidents, diff source commits against deployed artifacts, audit CI trigger permissions, and rotate all secrets accessible in affected developer and CI environments. For identity incidents, pull the full audit log for passkey registrations, recovery requests, device code authorization grants, and newly approved applications. Do not scope the investigation to the initial account: treat session token theft as potential full-tenant compromise and review conditional access policies and registered MFA methods across affected identities. The AhnLab ASEC report frames this as an IoA (Indicator of Attack) problem, where the behavior sequence matters more than individual file names or domains.

item.title: Linux Backdoors Impersonate Email Security Tools to Evade Detection in Korea and Taiwan
item.description:
Linux backdoors disguised as Korean and Taiwanese 🇹🇼 email security tools hit telecom and network appliances, blending malicious traffic into expected enterprise noise to frustrate detection.
Key details:
- Red Menshen (aka Earth Bluecrow, DecisiveArchitect, Red Dev 18) is behind a new BPFDoor variant and a BPF Rekoobe build targeting South Korean 🇰🇷 systems, while a previously unreported implant called AVERAT hits Taiwanese 🇹🇼 appliances. The distinguishing tradecraft here is regionalized process spoofing: BPFDoor samples impersonate the PID file of SpamSniper, rotate through ten Linux daemon names, or set their process name to "ora_ppmond" to blend into Oracle telecom environments. Rekoobe names its processes after SpamSniper components and listens on source and destination port 25 across TCP, UDP, SCTP IPv4, and UDP IPv6.
- The new BPFDoor variant adapts specifically to evade the Suricata and Snort signatures written after earlier public disclosures. Operators now wrap the magic packet in standard HTTPS POST requests and rely on SSL offloading common in telecom environments, allowing the trigger to reach the BPFDoor-infected node without tripping conventional deep packet inspection. Once triggered, BPFDoor launches a TinyShell session supporting interactive shell, upload, and download. TinyShell use overlaps with China-nexus clusters Liminal Panda, UNC3886 (Fire Ant), and Velvet Ant, all prior telecom and edge-device operators.
- AVERAT is an ELF dropper found inside ShareTech appliances at /addpkg/sbin/, the add-on package directory. The dropper derives its AES key from the string "ShareTech", decrypts a shell script that stages two binaries named "ntpdate" (the dropper) and "udevds" (the AVERAT payload), then deletes both 10 seconds after execution. AVERAT uses SMTP over TCP port 25 as its C2 channel, beaconing to mx.zxopfds[.]com every 600 to 699 seconds with the server address and interval stored in encrypted config. Its command set is extensive: directory enumeration, chunked file upload and download with resume, recursive deletion, process listing with full command lines, interactive shell with up to 10 concurrent sessions, port forwarding, runtime C2 table overwrite, and dynamic .so module loading to extend implant functionality.
- AVERAT's C2 infrastructure matches the device-class profile of an Operational Relay Box network, though Rapid7 found no evidence tying it to known ORBs such as LapDogs, SPACEHOP, or FLORAHOX. The pattern mirrors the 2023 UNC4841 campaign that exploited CVE-2023-2868 and CVE-2023-7102 in Barracuda Email Security Gateway appliances to plant persistent backdoors, reinforcing a pattern of China-nexus actors treating secure email gateways as privileged collection points.
Practitioner takeaway: On Linux appliances, audit for unexpected raw packet sockets and BPF filters using "ss -0p" and "bpftool prog list". Hunt outbound TCP port 25 connections from processes that are not mail services, starting with anything named "udevds" or "ntpdate" in non-standard paths. Check /proc/[pid]/exe and /proc/[pid]/cmdline for process name mismatches that impersonate legitimate daemons. For BPFDoor specifically, look for processes without open file descriptors on any listening port, as BPF passive listeners leave no socket in "netstat" output. The full IOC list is in the Rapid7 report.

item.title: ClickFix Attack Hides VBScript Payload in Browser Cache
item.description:
ClickFix campaign pre-fetches VBScript into browser cache disguised as an image file, bypassing the Windows Run dialog character limit and evading download-based detections entirely.
Key findings:
- The attack chain begins with compromised websites displaying a fake CAPTCHA that instructs victims to open the Windows Run dialog, paste a command from their clipboard, and press Enter. Critically, the VBScript payload was already on disk inside the browser cache before the victim acted. Sites pre-fetched it as a cached file, sidestepping network-based payload delivery detection.
- The pasted command launched cmd.exe, which enumerated the browser profile folder looking for cached files whose names began with "f_" and matched an expected file size. No content inspection or marker strings were used for identification, just a size comparison. The matched file was then copied to a temp folder, given a .vbs extension, and executed via wscript.exe. This size-matching pivot is a deliberate evasion step over earlier ClickFix variants.
- Post-execution, the VBScript used WMI to collect host details, retrieved a PowerShell script with execution policy bypassed, and compiled additional code loaded entirely in memory. That code was injected into the legitimate timeout.exe process for credential theft targeting browsers and the device itself. Later stages unpacked a Python interpreter using the built-in tar.exe and established persistence via a scheduled task running a Python payload through pythonw.exe, surviving reboots.
- Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects malicious command execution under this campaign as Trojan:Win32/ClickFix and Trojan:Win32/TermFix. The forensic footprint is spread across multiple artifact types: the RunMRU registry key (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU) captures what the victim typed or pasted into the Run dialog, browser cache folders hold the disguised payload, scheduled tasks and pythonw.exe execution reflect the persistence mechanism, and PowerShell script block logs (when enabled) capture the downloaded script content.
Responders hunting this campaign should pull RunMRU entries for unusual cmd.exe or file-path strings, review browser cache directories for .vbs or mismatched-extension files, query scheduled tasks for Python-based entries using tar.exe in their creation chain, and enable PowerShell script block logging immediately if it is not on. Parent-child chains of wscript.exe spawning PowerShell, and PowerShell spawning timeout.exe, are high-fidelity pivots. A CAPTCHA asking a user to execute code is always an attack, not a verification.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] RCDevs WebADM 2.4.14 authenticated log viewer sid command injection to webadm uid 999 code execution (7.2)
item.description:
RCDevs WebADM 2.4.14 carries an authenticated OS command injection in its admin log viewer, scoring CVSS 7.2 High, with no patch and no CVE assigned as of public disclosure on 5 October 2026.
Key findings:
- The sink is admin/logfile_viewer.php, which interpolates the sid GET parameter directly into a shell command: grep -E 'sid' logfile | tail -n 10000, passed to PHP's popen() with no escapeshellarg, no escapeshellcmd, no allow-list and no length cap. A single apostrophe closes the quoted grep pattern and everything after it executes as shell text. The root cause is the complete absence of any filter, not a bypass of one. CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H.
- Exploitation requires a console administrator session (PR:H). The out-of-band execution channel matters here: the endpoint does not echo command output in the HTTP response. The injected command writes to /opt/webadm/logs/webadm.log and the same viewer reads that file back over HTTPS when a different log selector is requested, making the finding self-verifying. Commands run as uid=999(webadm) gid=999(webadm) with no privilege drop configured.
- From uid 999 the blast radius covers the full authorization domain the application already holds: read and rewrite of platform config under /opt/webadm (persistence that survives a service restart), access to the local LDAP and MariaDB listeners using credentials the application carries (user records, OTP state, second-factor enrolments), interaction with the certificate signing daemon from inside its trust boundary, and log writes enabling both anti-forensics and the observation channel the exploit itself uses.
- Two detection traps to carry into any rule: every /admin/*.php request returns HTTP 200 with the WebADM doctype regardless of session state, so HTTP status codes and response lengths are not usable as authorization signals. Detect on shell metacharacters, especially the apostrophe, in the sid parameter, and on unstructured lines appearing in /opt/webadm/logs/webadm.log. Process ancestry alone is weak: webadm-httpd spawning grep and tail is normal viewer behaviour.
- No CVE has been assigned. The vendor (RCDevs Security SA) was notified through their general contact mailbox. No security.txt, no VDP, no researcher intake channel exists, so disclosure was unconditional and simultaneous. Only WebADM 2.4.14 Freeware Edition was tested; other versions and licensed editions with additional modules are unclaimed.
Practitioner takeaway: Until a patch lands, bind the admin vhost to a management interface or VPN, treat console administrator credentials as tier-zero secrets behind a second factor, and alert on apostrophes or other shell metacharacters in sid query parameters in your web server or WAF logs. On suspicion of exploitation, rotate the administrator, LDAP, and database credentials immediately and audit second-factor enrolments for the window in question. The report includes a full technical analysis with a reproducible proof-of-concept and a disposition table of the 11 unauthenticated endpoints examined.

item.title: You Won’t Hear About These, Even In Myths (Atlassian Jira, Confluence (and more) Pre-Auth Arbitrary File Read CVE-2026-21589)
item.description:
CVE-2026-21589: Pre-auth arbitrary file read in the shared atlassian-plugins-webresource JAR hits every major Atlassian Data Center product, and in Crowd-integrated deployments it chains to full administrative takeover with no credentials required.
Key findings:
- The root cause lives in a single shared library, atlassian-plugins-webresource-6.0.7.jar, specifically in Router[.]java inside com/atlassian/plugin/webresource/impl/http/Router.java. The escapeSlashes and unescapeSlashes functions swap forward slashes for double colons and back again. Attackers weaponize this with a path traversal payload using the :: delimiter instead of the classic ../: a request like GET /download/resources/jira.webresources:color-picker-popup/images/..::..::..::..::..::WEB-INF::web.xml to {{Jira-Hostname}} reads files from within the Tomcat application root without any authentication. The deprecated getResourceRelativeToWebResource function in ResourceServingHelpers[.]java still processes user-controlled resourceName values and passes them to createResourceWithRelativePath, where path sanitization in splitLastPathPart is bypassed by the :: primitive. Bitbucket uses a slightly different route: GET /s/1.0/_/download/resources/com.atlassian.bitbucket.server.bitbucket-webpack-INTERNAL:avatar/avatar/..::..::..::..::..::WEB-INF::urlrewrite[.]xml.
- The critical escalation path runs through Atlassian Crowd integration. When Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, or Bamboo are configured to use Crowd for SSO and centralized auth (which Atlassian recommends), the Crowd application credentials are stored in plaintext at WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties including application[.]name, application.password, and the Crowd server URL. Reading that file via the traversal hands an attacker authenticated access to the Crowd REST API. From there, creating a rogue admin is three API calls: enumerate users at /crowd/rest/usermanagement/1/search, create an account at /crowd/rest/usermanagement/1/user, then POST to /crowd/rest/usermanagement/1/group/user/direct?groupname=jira-administrators. Full compromise, no prior access needed.
- Scope is severe. All prior versions of Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, and Fisheye Data Center are affected. Watchtowr estimates six to seven figures of vulnerable instances based on internet exposure alone, with Confluence showing just under 700,000 exposed instances in open search. Fixed versions are product-specific: Jira Software Data Center 9.12.40, 10.3.26, or 11.3.12; Confluence Data Center 9.2.26 or 10.2.19; Bitbucket Data Center 9.4.26, 10.2.8, or 10.5.1; Bamboo 10.2.24 or 12.1.12; Crowd 6.3.7, 7.0.3, 7.1.7, or 7.2.4; Jira Service Management 5.12.40, 10.3.26, or 11.3.12; Crucible and Fisheye 4.9.15.
- Detection artifacts to hunt now: look in your web or reverse-proxy access logs for GET requests containing :: sequences in the path, especially against /download/resources/, /s/1/_/download/resources/, and /s/1.0/_/download/resources/ endpoints. The Atlassian-supplied WAF regex targets :: combined with .. and path separators. In application logs, look for unexpected reads of WEB-INF/web.xml, WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties, or WEB-INF/urlrewrite.xml. On the Crowd side, hunt for new user creations and group membership changes via the REST API in Crowd's audit log, particularly accounts added to jira-administrators, confluence-administrators, or similar high-privilege groups in a short window after an unusual file-read request.
Patch to the fixed versions immediately. Before you do, check WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties and rotate application.password for every Crowd-connected application unconditionally: if this has been exploited, that credential is burned. Review Crowd's audit log for unexpected user creations or group assignments going back at least 30 days. Atlassian's advisory includes WAF rules. Watchtowr has published a Detection Artefact Generator covering Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket to confirm whether an instance is vulnerable; the report links it directly.

item.title: Logging is a Discipline, Not a Switch
item.description:
Active Directory logging gaps expose defenders during intrusions. TrustedSec's practical guide walks through building a logging program that would actually catch an attacker, not just generate data.
Key findings:
- Log container size is the first failure point. The Security log default of 20MB on domain controllers is dangerously small. CIS recommends a minimum of 192MB (196,608KB) for Security and 32MB for Application, Setup, and System logs. Before any audit policy change, set "Control Event Log behavior when the log file reaches its maximum size" to Disabled (retain rolling behavior) via Group Policy at Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates, and verify on-box retention outlasts any collector maintenance window.
- Advanced Audit Policy must override legacy categories. Enable "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings" under Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options. The report publishes a full subcategory matrix comparing TrustedSec and CIS Benchmark (Windows Server 2025 v2.1.0) recommendations. Notable divergences: TrustedSec adds Audit DPAPI Activity (Success and Failure) and Audit Directory Service Access (Success and Failure) where CIS flags only Failure; CIS adds file share and removable storage auditing that TrustedSec omits. Blend both for full coverage, and roll changes out incrementally to avoid log balloon and event overwrite before ingestion.
- Ten detection goals frame what the telemetry must cover: authentication anomalies (password spraying, impossible travel), privileged account and group membership changes, process execution with command lines (LOLBAS binaries), PowerShell script block logging including AMSI bypass and IEX patterns, DNS query logs for newly registered domains, firewall egress for unexpected large outbound transfers, domain controller identity telemetry covering Kerberoasting, AS-REP Roasting, and DCSync signatures, email gateway telemetry, web proxy logs, and security tool evasion signals including EDR agent stops, event log clears, and new services or scheduled tasks.
- Sysmon fills native logging gaps, but only after the fundamentals are stable. Process hashes, network connections by process, image loads, and named pipes are invisible to native audit policy alone. A tuned configuration is mandatory before deployment.

A domain controller that rolls its Security log in under 24 hours loses evidence before any collector can ingest it. Active Directory logging gaps expose defenders during intrusions. TrustedSec's practical guide walks through building a logging program that would actually catch an attacker, not just generate data.

Key findings:

- Log container size is the first failure point. The Security log default of 20MB on domain controllers is dangerously small. Before any audit policy change, set "Control Event Log behavior when the log file reaches its maximum size" to Disabled (retain rolling behavior) via Group Policy at Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates, and verify on-box retention outlasts any collector maintenance window.

- Advanced Audit Policy must override legacy categories. Enable "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings" under Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options. item.title: Update on Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772: Expanded THOR Detection Coverage
item.description:
Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 exploitation is broader and deeper than initially reported, with post-exploitation chains covering webshells, bind shells, C2 frameworks, and direct config tampering observed in the wild.
Key findings:
- The full post-exploitation chain recovered from compromised NetScaler systems includes Apache config modification to enable PHP processing, webshell deployment, Perl-based bind shells launched from temp directories, hidden payload downloads, chmod abuse on /bin/sh for privilege escalation, and creation of a privileged account named sec_monitor with superuser rights written into ns.conf. Each of those stages has a named detection rule in this update: MAL_CVE_2026_88771_NetScaler_Webshell_Dropper_Oct26, MAL_CVE_2026_88771_Perl_BindShell_Oct26, SUSP_Chmod_BinSh_Priv_Escalation_Oct26, and SUSP_CVE_2026_88771_User_Creation_Oct26 among others.
- Platypus, an open-source fleet management framework, was observed being abused as C2 infrastructure. Bootstrap scripts download, prepare, and execute the compiled Platypus agent. Two rules cover this: PUA_Platypus_Oct26 for the agent binary itself, and MAL_Platypus_C2_Agent_Bootstrap_Oct26 for the retrieval and launch scripts. Platypus abuse on edge appliances is a significant escalation: it hands the attacker persistent, interactive C2 with minimal footprint.
- Named malware families SLAPSHOT (tunneler) and WHIPSHOT (backdoor webshell) are covered by EXT_MAL_G_APT_Tunneler_SLAPSHOT_1_Sep26 and EXT_MAL_G_APT_Backdoorwebshell_WHIPSHOT_1_Sep26. Separate rules target scripts that unbind VPN and authentication policies and modify the default EPA group, covering attacker attempts to disable NetScaler endpoint security checks entirely (MAL_CVE_2026_88771_NetScaler_EPA_Bypass_Oct26).
- The report tested 21 new campaign-specific rules plus 24 pre-existing generic rules against a 50-artifact sample set. Every artifact was matched by at least one rule, and many matched several simultaneously because a single post-exploitation script often bundles exploitation logic, persistence, privilege escalation, and webshell deployment together. Pre-existing generic rules like SUSP_Linux_Downloader_Jul20_1, SUSP_Webshell_Keywords_Apr21, and MAL_Webshell_Citrix_CVE_2023_3519_Aug23_1 are still firing, which confirms generic coverage predates the campaign-specific rules and should not be disabled.
- For responders without an agent already on the appliance, the report describes two practical scanning approaches: mount the NetScaler filesystem remotely via SSHFS over port 22/tcp and scan from a Linux host (expect 30 to 60 minutes per appliance and significant network traffic), or deploy a lightweight scheduled collector that pushes newly created or modified files to a central scanning service over HTTPS, avoiding persistent inbound SSH. The second model is recommended for recurring assessments of internet-facing appliances.
Takeaway: On any NetScaler system that was internet-exposed during this campaign window, start your triage by hunting ns.conf for the sec_monitor account and superuser assignments, check Apache config for unexpected PHP handler additions, and look in temp directories for Perl scripts and recently downloaded binaries. The EPA bypass leaves traces in policy binding state: compare current VPN and authentication policy bindings against a known-good baseline. The full set of 21 new rules and named IOCs are in the Nextron report, and both SSHFS and collector-based scan methods are documented there for appliances where direct agent deployment is not feasible.

item.title: Up a Creek Without a Command Line: Mapping an Akira Ransomware Attack
item.description:
Akira ransomware dissected without EDR: Huntress reconstructs a full attack chain using Shellbags, PowerShell event logs, and Akira's own log files after a post-compromise agent install left the early stages dark.
Key findings:
- Initial access came via RDP from a workstation named C1IFRYXI, not owned by the victim org. The threat actor immediately hit the BitDefender console and stopped four endpoint security services (Endpoint Update, Integration, Protected, and Security) before dropping procdump.exe into C:\PerfLogs to dump lsass credentials. The attack staging folder throughout was C:\PerfLogs, worth flagging as a hunt target on its own.
- With no process telemetry for the ransomware execution itself, analysts correlated three artifact classes as a composite signal: Shellbags confirmed the threat actor browsed target Share subfolders via Windows Explorer immediately before and after each encryption run; PowerShell event logs showed "Get-WmiObject Win32_Shadowcopy | Remove-WmiObject" firing at the same moment; and Akira's own log file was created at that timestamp pointing at the same folder. The same sequence repeated four times across four Share subfolders, the threat actor manually verifying encryption success each time.
- GOST tunnel (Go Simple Tunnel) was deployed roughly four hours into the encryption phase, running as svchost.exe from C:\PerfLogs\temp\ under SYSTEM, loading config.dll, and beaconing to 64.227.4[.]134. GOST svchost.exe SHA256: d00833318a04caa019c6f95dcb3598ad947d405010bfb2f3cbd04530a00bc3a4. RClone followed from the same staging folder for data exfiltration to cloud storage.
- Ransomware binary at C:\storage\win.exe SHA256: 1f1bb322591b6d27fd2946e373d7d2efc2f4e1e66818846060d391600b600fba. The Akira log files the ransomware itself generated became forensic evidence against it, correlating execution time, target paths, and the VSS deletion command to reconstruct a timeline the EDR never captured.
Takeaway: When EDR telemetry starts mid-attack, treat Shellbags (NTUSER.DAT), PowerShell operational logs (Event ID 4104), and application-generated logs as a triad. Shellbags show where the actor navigated and when; PowerShell logs capture the VSS wipe command that confirms ransomware launch even without a recorded ransomware command line; and the malware's own log file timestamps the target. Hunt C:\PerfLogs for unsigned executables, new DLLs, and child processes under svchost. Full IOC list is in the report.

item.title: Beyond valid credentials: How exposed AWS keys are tested for Amazon Bedrock access
item.description:
Credential harvesting platform KMON_NOC has been actively probing AWS environments for Bedrock-capable keys since August 31, 2026, while two Python scripts on VirusTotal reveal the exact API call chain attackers use to validate and monetize stolen LLM access.
Key findings:
- KMON_NOC is a credential harvesting platform observed scanning over 80 Cloud SIEM customers. Its frontend JavaScript bundle exposes a dedicated validation pipeline: STS GetCallerIdentity first confirms a key is live, then a separate Bedrock check populates a keysWithBedrock counter displayed on the operator dashboard. The platform also extracts the AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK environment variable directly, targeting Bedrock-native credentials in addition to general-purpose IAM keys. The platform routes validation through proxies using Signature Version 4 signing, complicating source attribution.
- Two Python scripts on VirusTotal (SHA-256: c9335bb8a21bd2c568d03b040fb86a0e72145691e54a33495ee0cfaac55835dc and 923641364ef0ce3a6f1d944890244082b8c7f29c9600c0433b2a0ca9822c0608) automate the full validation chain: GetCallerIdentity to confirm key validity, ListFoundationModels across multiple regions to map available models and providers, ListInferenceProfiles, and then a Bedrock runtime Converse call with the prompt "ping" capped at four tokens to minimize inference cost during bulk testing. Successful credentials are written to disk in plaintext.
- The second script adds billing:GetCredits enumeration, calling the Billing API to extract remaining credit balances, currency, expiration dates, and whether credits apply to Bedrock specifically. This lets the attacker assess not just whether a key works but how much free runway exists before the victim's account incurs charges, directly informing resale value. Comments in the code suggest it may have been written or assisted by an LLM.
- In the last 30 days, Datadog observed 12 organizations showing this behavior in telemetry. The most common pattern is failed ListFoundationModels calls across multiple regions, consistent with credential testing against locked-down accounts. One confirmed case showed successful multi-region ListFoundationModels and ListInferenceProfiles calls followed by Converse attempts against anthropic.claude-opus-5, anthropic.claude-fable-5, and anthropic.claude-fable-5-1, all returning AccessDenied. This mirrors the script's logic exactly.
Hunt tip: In CloudTrail, alert on any identity calling ListFoundationModels or ListInferenceProfiles with no prior history of Bedrock usage, especially across multiple regions in a short window. A "ping" Converse call with maxTokens set to 4 is a near-certain indicator of credential validation, not legitimate use. Pair GetCallerIdentity events from unfamiliar source IPs with subsequent Bedrock control-plane calls to build a high-confidence detection. The full IOC list including both script hashes and over 60 IP addresses associated with this campaign (residential proxies, VPNs, and hosting providers) is in the Datadog Security Labs report.

item.title: More RMM Tools In the Wild, (Tue, Oct 6th)
item.description:
Phishing campaign abuses Action1 RMM agent for persistent remote access, dropping a signed MSI via PDF redirect and VBS. No EDR detections on VirusTotal at time of discovery.
Key findings:
- The attack chain starts with a phishing email carrying a fake PDF invoice. The PDF uses an OpenAction and URI object to silently redirect the victim's browser to hxxps://up-theta-rose.vercel[.]app/adobe_new_update.vbs when opened, keeping the malicious URL out of the email body entirely and bypassing link-scanning controls. The VBS itself is unobfuscated and displays a clean decoy PDF as a distraction while the real payload downloads.
- The VBS fetches hxxps://up-theta-rose.vercel[.]app/action1.msi, a packaged installer for the legitimate Action1 RMM agent. The four files inside carry these SHA-256 hashes: a1_7z_dll_file (eaff35d250c9b04f51c971e70082740dbfeee5dd846829d541f588ad43378727), a1_sas_dll_file (996b01e15f85e165899630721a141b178a9c372b6e878012180ec9e9d4e7bd06), action1_remote_exe (1b19115d5ebdc216e0ab3adf2c643648cfc70a385f4caf0217c679f9f3b20342), and main_service_exe (941695d20d82dd5d62f74b0111feb23720637202f6c797df2a02e2cb6cb6e8e3). All four were clean on VirusTotal at discovery, meaning file-reputation defenses offer no protection here.
- Persistence is established as a Windows service named A1Agent ("Action1 Agent"), executing C:\Windows\Action1\action1_agent.exe. The registry key HKLM\Software\Action1\Agent holds the values CustomerId, Certificate, PrivateKey, MSI, and INSTALLDIR. The CustomerID observed is 49b18106-681d-456a-b098-092e2818c09a, and the agent beacons out to server[.]na-2.action1[.]com, the legitimate Action1 cloud infrastructure. The MSI is signed with a valid "Action1 Corporation" certificate, though the signing cert expired in May 2026.
- This is the same playbook seen days earlier with ScreenConnect: a threat actor registers a free or trial account with a legitimate RMM vendor, then uses that vendor's own cloud infrastructure as the C2 relay. Because the traffic goes to a known, signed, whitelisted service endpoint, network-layer detections rarely fire. The attacker gets persistent, interactive remote access with no custom implant to detect.
Hunt for the A1Agent service name and the action1_agent.exe process in your environment. Check HKLM\Software\Action1\Agent for unexpected CustomerID values and correlate any outbound connections to action1[.]com against your known asset inventory. PDF files triggering browser navigation on open, followed by a VBS fetch from a Vercel-hosted URL, are a strong pre-infection signal worth building a detection around. The SANS ISC diary carries the full file hashes listed above.

item.title: IronChain Ransomware Threatens Businesses with Permanent Data Loss and Costly Downtime
item.description:
IronChain ransomware carries a wiper-like encryption design that discards its own recovery keys, making payment technically meaningless. A September 2026 build adds four kernel drivers and SYSTEM-level persistence to an already destructive package.
Key findings:
- The September 12 build (SHA-256 09b550d66b7ce269fa577edcac54d6ba3e0f3cb5b660a2921b9372d37d52e254) is a 9.7 MB unsigned PyInstaller x64 PE compiled 42 seconds before its first VirusTotal submission. At startup it generates an RSA-4096 keypair and immediately discards the private component, keeping only the public key. Each file gets a 32-byte AES key wrapped with RSA-OAEP, then subjected to two to seven randomized byte-mutation passes before AES-GCM encryption. Both the RSA private key and the random mutation state are gone by the time the ransom note appears. Even a working decryptor could not guarantee exact reversal. This is ransomware presentation over wiper-grade design.
- Four kernel drivers are bundled: Baidu BdApiUtil.sys (d8ce0a5866178495a66d23c9587822164966111fcd34764011e907951c599711), Safetica ProcessMonitorDriver.sys 11.26.18 (5b4f59236a9b950bcd5191b35d19125f60cfb9e1a1e1aa2e4f914b6745dde9df), Lenovo LnvMSRIO.sys 3.1.0.29 stored as BootRepair.sys (977d3b78bdf5723430e2e21cf1eb515a2335a0e370c76fa2dda4315ba062f429), and ThrottleStop 3.0.0.0 (16f83f056177c4ec24c7e99d01ca9d9d6713bd0497eeedb777a3ffefa99c97f0). Only the Baidu path forms a coherent BYOVD-style process-kill chain: IronChain opens \\.\BdApiUtil, sends IOCTL 0x800024B4 with a four-byte PID, and the driver routes through PsLookupProcessByProcessId and ZwTerminateProcess. Safetica is rejected by both a wrong IOCTL (0xB822200C vs. 0xB822A00C) and insufficient input length. The Lenovo driver creates \\.\WinMsrDev but IronChain requests \\.\BootRepair, a mismatch that blocks use entirely. The ThrottleStop IOCTL 0x8000649C appears in configuration but no call site ever sends it. CVE-2024-51324, CVE-2025-70795, CVE-2025-8061, and CVE-2025-7771 are relevant to these driver families per the report, but IronChain only successfully speaks the Baidu interface.
- Persistence and defense impairment are well-documented in sandbox telemetry. IronChain creates a scheduled task named IronChain_SYSTEM with SYSTEM privileges, attempts firewall shutdown, and tries to stop or disable EventLog and Resmon. A bare Python exception handler accidentally consumes sys.exit() calls, keeping the original process alive through UAC elevation, SYSTEM task launch, and relocation, so overlapping privileged processes are possible. A separate variable naming bug (local _rt vs. undefined global rt) raises NameError and skips the broader file traversal covering Windows directories, AppData, and non-C drives, narrowing encryption to common user folders: Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Pictures, Videos, and Music across a 48-worker pool.
- For large files IronChain encrypts the first 512,000 bytes, a random 51,200-byte middle chunk, and the final 512,000 bytes, leaving plaintext gaps. Those gaps, unallocated space, shadow copies, and memory remnants are worth examining during response. The ransom portal is ironchaindecrypt7xfzq5tclm9jzpwq72uofgy2znkdsxm54zbcu2yid[.]onion. The IP 103.224.182.251 received no response in sandbox testing and is not confirmed C2. ip-api[.]com requests are for geolocation display in the ransom UI, not operator infrastructure.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for the combined pattern: scheduled task IronChain_SYSTEM, kernel services BdApiUtil, STProcessMonitor, LenovoBootRepair, and ThrottleStop appearing together, Lenovo driver content written as LenovoBootRepair.sys, the file marker CHAINED_6617-382+819=, and artifacts IronChain.hta, IronChainBg.bmp, and %ProgramData%\IRONCHAIN\time.dat. If IronChain is suspected, isolate from networks and removable media before rebooting since raw writes to \\.\PhysicalDrive0 may have occurred. Preserve memory and disk images. The report includes a YARA rule and four Sigma documents covering these clusters.

item.content:encoded:
IronChain ransomware carries a wiper-like encryption design that discards its own recovery keys, making payment technically meaningless. A September 2026 build adds four kernel drivers and SYSTEM-level persistence to an already destructive package.

Key findings:

- The September 12 build (SHA-256 09b550d66b7ce269fa577edcac54d6ba3e0f3cb5b660a2921b9372d37d52e254) is a 9.7 MB unsigned PyInstaller x64 PE compiled 42 seconds before its first VirusTotal submission. At startup it generates an RSA-4096 keypair and immediately discards the private component, keeping only the public key. Each file gets a 32-byte AES key wrapped with RSA-OAEP, then subjected to two to seven randomized byte-mutation passes before AES-GCM encryption. Both the RSA private key and the random mutation state are gone by the time the ransom note appears. Even a working decryptor could not guarantee exact reversal. This is ransomware presentation over wiper-grade design.

- Four kernel drivers are bundled: Baidu BdApiUtil.sys (d8ce0a5866178495a66d23c9587822164966111fcd34764011e907951c599711), Safetica ProcessMonitorDriver.sys 11.26.18 (5b4f59236a9b950bcd5191b35d19125f60cfb9e1a1e1aa2e4f914b6745dde9df), Lenovo LnvMSRIO.sys 3.1.0.29 stored as BootRepair.sys (977d3b78bdf5723430e2e21cf1eb515a2335a0e370c76fa2dda4315ba062f429), and ThrottleStop 3.0.0.0 (16f83f056177c4ec24c7e99d01ca9d9d6713bd0497eeedb777a3ffefa99c97f0). item.title: Blinder Tunnel Campaign Targets Iraqi Infrastructure
item.description:
Iranian 🇮🇷 state-aligned actor CL-STA-1178 targets Iraqi critical infrastructure using trojanized Visual Studio coding challenges, GitHub dead-drop C2, and Chisel tunneling in the "Blinder Tunnel" campaign active since March 2026.
Key findings:
- The infection chain begins with a fake Dubai Airports recruitment lure delivering DubaiAirport_Carrers_IT_Test.zip, a weaponized Visual Studio project that fires the moment a developer opens it in their IDE. Visual Studio's design-time build invokes msbuild.exe, which executes the attacker's custom GetFrameworkPaths XML target in FlightManager.csproj before any compile step. This drops malicious binaries into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\RuntimeBrokers\ and launches RuntimeBroker.exe, a renamed vshost.exe. AppDomainManager hijacking via RuntimeBroker.exe.config then forces the .NET runtime to cede control to ShelbyLoader V2, while the directive disables ETW entirely, impairing in-memory threat visibility before the RAT runs.
- The malware stack is modular: ShelbyLoader V2 (RuntimeBroker.dll, SHA-256 53f35e49eb9b271fd8cbcd3daacb525328dbf159a03dbd1c7adebe0363daa402) handles persistence via HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\MicrosoftRuntime and beacons every 63 seconds to the peakyblinders-tm/myLic GitHub repository using a hard-coded Personal Access Token. ShelbyC2 V2 (RuntimeBrokerApi.dll) is the primary RAT, PsProxy.dll executes PowerShell inside a custom runspace without spawning PowerShell.exe, and Blackwood.dll reflectively loads a Go-compiled Chisel binary from an AES-256-CBC-encrypted 8.4 MB manifest resource to establish a reverse SOCKS5 tunnel (R:0.0.0.0:10999:socks) to 91.107.156[.]29. All binaries are obfuscated with Obfuscar.
- C2 resilience is built around GitHub as living-off-the-cloud infrastructure. The primary channel uses the GitHub API to read and write files in a private repo. On HTTP 401, ShelbyLoader V2 pivots to the GitHub Issues Search API, querying by date (yyyymmdd), extracting AES-256-CBC ciphertext hidden inside HTML comment markers in issue bodies, and deriving the decryption key from an MD5 of the date concatenated with a unique machineId seeded from the string "Peaky Blinders 2.1". This rotates C2 owner, repo path, and token dynamically. GitHub accounts to hunt: hxxps[:]//github[.]com/peakyblinders-tm and hxxps[:]//github[.]com/GreenBeret0.
- Attribution rests on layered forensic artifacts, not just TTPs. The Blackwood C2 IP 87.248.129[.]239 is hosted by Iranian 🇮🇷 ISP TOSE'EH ERTEBATAT NOVIN ARIA. Passive DNS for 91.107.156[.]29 resolves to subdomains under ns1.soroshpasargad[.]com via a likely Iranian 🇮🇷 reseller. The peakyblinders-tm GitHub README embedded Peaky Blinders Team.mp3 with a COMMENT metadata field retaining MusicDel[.]ir, a domestic Iranian 🇮🇷 music platform, indicating the operators never stripped file metadata before publishing. A parallel May-June 2026 credential-harvesting campaign against an Israeli 🇮🇱 entity used Google-typosquat domains (cloud.g-drive[.]cam, googeldrive[.]cam, drivegoogel[.]cam, googelmeet[.]online, meetonline[.]cam) hosted on 65.109.214[.]145, linked to Blinder Tunnel infrastructure through shared Blackwood samples.
- Detection anchors: watch for msbuild.exe or Visual Studio spawning unexpected child processes or writing binaries to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\RuntimeBrokers\. Flag vshost.exe or vshost32.exe executing outside their standard install paths and loading non-Microsoft DLLs via DLL search-order. Hunt for .NET processes making authenticated HTTPS calls to api.github[.]com with Bearer tokens, especially reading or writing content paths matching /{hex16}/Lic.txt or /{hex16}/Inf.txt patterns. The ETW-disable directive in any .exe.config file is a high-fidelity indicator. For the tunneling stage, look for Go-compiled binaries loaded reflectively from .NET processes and outbound connections to 91.107.156[.]29, 87.248.129[.]239, 65.109.214[.]145, and 38.180.136[.]127 on non-standard ports.
Full IOC list including hashes, IPs, phishing domains, GitHub infrastructure, and the registry persistence key are in the Unit 42 report. Infrastructure was staged from November 2025 before activation in March 2026, so treat that window as the earliest forensic boundary for any affected organization.

item.title: CITRIX 0-DAY EXPLOITS: CVE-2026-88771 & CVE-2026-88772 IN THE WILD
item.description:
CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 hit Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway with CVSS 9.5, actively exploited in the wild since September 29, 2026. A full post-exploitation toolkit: SLAPSHOT tunneler, WHIPSHOT web shell, and Platypus C2 agent deployed on compromised appliances.
- CVE-2026-88771 (unauthenticated RCE via improper input validation) and CVE-2026-88772 (UDP memory overflow leading to RCE or DoS) are the two of eight assigned CVEs confirmed exploited in the wild, both carrying CVSS 9.5. Exploitation is not single-step: CVE-2026-88771 works by sending crafted strings into authentication endpoints like /nf/auth/doAuthentication.do, which get written into NetScaler logs and later executed as root by the internal maintenance script ns_monuploadd_err.pl. CVE-2026-88772 targets the DTLS stack over UDP to overflow a memory buffer without touching logs or scripts at all. Attackers chain both simultaneously as a backup strategy since appliance configuration determines which surface is reachable. Mass scanning began September 29 and GreyNoise confirms high scanner volume from that date onward, with active exploit IPs including 103.62.49[.]154, 37.19.221[.]171, 66.42.100[.]63, and 213.209.159[.]55 (primary SLAPSHOT C2).
- Once root is obtained, a Perl-based installer (Pitboss Shell, MD5: bb724df37959c23a4ce6b5c5c374217e, SHA-1: fae85e4e10dda2f25cd023bf8e2e61432d33a7f5, SHA-256: 974b69782fdf5d67b97cfd508465939e44ee10798dbcc1e82b92d78776bad938) executes a six-stage persistence chain: creates rogue superuser sec_monitor (password ay#39&RGYvv4Xuzy) written directly into /flash/nsconfig/ns.conf, sets SUID on /bin/sh via chmod 06555, tarballs /flash/nsconfig to /tmp/update_result_3567cs.tgz and exfiltrates it via HTTP POST to 64.94.85[.]67:443, drops WHIPSHOT PHP web shell as /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/.local_journal (password: QI@UEG5PC7oRt31E, SHA-256 stored hash: e4d909c290d0fb1ca068ffaddf22cbd0), patches /etc/httpd.conf to execute .deb, .sig, .ico, and .local_journal as PHP, and aliases the shell to the legitimate-looking path /logon/LogonPoint/css/LogonUISimple.html.style.min.css. A backup of the original httpd.conf is written to /etc/httpd.conf.slap.bak. The installer then self-deletes and sends HUP to Apache.
- SLAPSHOT is the post-exploitation tunneler: a multi-threaded Python 3 session manager (slapshot[.]py at /var/tmp/.ux/slapshot.py) combined with a Perl TCP multiplexer (agent[.]pl at /nsconfig/.slap/agent.pl) that listens only on loopback and opens arbitrary outbound TCP connections from the appliance's own IP, making pivot traffic look like normal ADC traffic. Web shell receivers disguised as CSS files or hidden files (.ctxs.receiver, .slap.receiver, receiver.deb) sit in /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/. SLAPSHOT auth token: 072874c28950cf7befd319d17e9709e7. The report identifies 33 SLAPSHOT samples, with C2 URLs under hxxp://213.209.159[.]55:443/t/ and hxxp://213.209.159[.]55:80/t/. A Platypus C2 agent was also recovered, downloading from entretiensol[.]com via hxxps://entretiensol[.]com:443/api/v1/install/ paths, with Platypus token plt_2uhfcg6a7npuwiuaiakb.w6rgc3kclkuwh7nhgr2h.
- Key filesystem artifacts to hunt on any NetScaler appliance: /nsconfig/.slap/ directory (SLAPSHOT install), /var/tmp/.ux/ (secondary SLAPSHOT directory), /tmp/.uxdport and /tmp/.uxdlock (runtime files), /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/.local_journal (WHIPSHOT shell), /var/tmp/.ns_data and /var/core/.ns-cache/ (Platypus working directories), and /etc/httpd.conf.slap.bak (evidence of httpd.conf tampering). In ns.conf, look for lines adding sec_monitor with superuser 100 binding. Check /bin/sh permissions for SUID (mode 6555). Review NetScaler logs for crafted strings injected via /nf/auth/doAuthentication.do and cross-reference with ns_monuploadd_err.pl execution timestamps.
Affected versions requiring immediate patching: NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1 prior to 14.1-73.36, 13.1 prior to 13.1-64.22, and all 14.1-FIPS and 13.1-FIPS/NDcPP builds prior to 14.1-73.37 FIPS and 13.1-37.279. Target fixed builds 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23. Beyond patching: the full IOC list including 150+ exploitation IPs, 33 SLAPSHOT sample hashes, 6 Platypus-communicating sample hashes, all C2 URLs, credentials, tokens, file paths, and a YARA detection rule are in the report. Pull those IOCs and check your NetScaler appliances for the filesystem indicators above before assuming you were not hit.

item.title: Cling botnet uses STUN traffic to conceal command-and-control activity and attacks against vulnerable IoT devices
item.description:
Cling botnet disguises C2 inside STUN protocol traffic and spoofs Google's STUN service to hide commands, exploiting CVE-2021-35394 and six other IoT flaws to spread and launch DDoS attacks.
Key findings:
- Cling exploits CVE-2021-35394, an RCE in the Realtek Jungle SDK diagnostic component (compiled as UDPServer) found in routers, access points, repeaters, and embedded appliances that rarely receive firmware updates. The malware also carries exploit code for six additional CVEs: CVE-2014-8361 (Realtek SDK), CVE-2023-26801 (LB-LINK routers), CVE-2024-3721 (TBK DVR), CVE-2025-34037 (Linksys), CVE-2016-10372 (Eir D1000), CVE-2023-41011 (FiberHome/China Mobile), and CVE-2016-20016 (MVPower CCTV DVR), giving it a wide propagation surface across commodity networking and surveillance hardware.
- The C2 design encodes operator commands inside STUN transaction IDs, sending traffic that resembles routine NAT-traversal exchanges from tools like Microsoft Teams, Zoom, and WebRTC browsers. Infected devices contact a hardcoded list of 13 STUN servers; one of them, confirmed operator-controlled at 145.249.115[.]184, receives bot registrations containing infection metadata and reachability info.
- Commands appear to originate from an IP belonging to Google's stun.l[.]google[.]com service. Nozomi's analysis points to source-address spoofing through a network provider that does not validate source addresses. TTL differences between genuine STUN replies and command-bearing packets are one of the few network-level tells that something is wrong.
- Observed commands included internet-wide scanning for additional vulnerable targets, TCP tunneling, proxying, and UDP/TCP flood attacks. Confirmed DDoS targets included a South Korean 🇰🇷 ISP, a University of Chicago cluster, and two Minecraft servers.
- Host artifacts are concrete and huntable: malware copies named .cling, persistence entries written to init scripts, and a replaced wget binary with companion files named wget.r and wget.p. Because most compromised devices offer no EDR telemetry, these filesystem indicators and network-layer patterns are often the only evidence available.
Detection priority: at the network layer, hunt for STUN Binding Requests sent at short, regular intervals with transaction IDs set to all zeros, and for non-STUN UDP datagrams directed at known STUN endpoints. At the host layer, scan internet-facing embedded devices for files named .cling, modified init scripts, and replaced wget binaries. Reputation alone cannot be trusted here as packets sourced from high-reputation infrastructure are exactly what the operator is manufacturing. The full IOC list and ATT&CK mapping are in the Nozomi Networks Labs report.

item.content:encoded:
Cling botnet disguises C2 inside STUN protocol traffic and spoofs Google's STUN service to hide commands, exploiting CVE-2021-35394 and six other IoT flaws to spread and launch DDoS attacks.

Key findings:

- Cling exploits CVE-2021-35394, an RCE in the Realtek Jungle SDK diagnostic component (compiled as UDPServer) found in routers, access points, repeaters, and embedded appliances that rarely receive firmware updates. The malware also carries exploit code for six additional CVEs: CVE-2014-8361 (Realtek SDK), CVE-2023-26801 (LB-LINK routers), CVE-2024-3721 (TBK DVR), CVE-2025-34037 (Linksys), CVE-2016-10372 (Eir D1000), CVE-2023-41011 (FiberHome/China Mobile), and CVE-2016-20016 (MVPower CCTV DVR), giving it a wide propagation surface across commodity networking and surveillance hardware.

- The C2 design encodes operator commands inside STUN transaction IDs, sending traffic that resembles routine NAT-traversal exchanges from tools like Microsoft Teams, Zoom, and WebRTC browsers. Infected devices contact a hardcoded list of 13 STUN servers; one of them, confirmed operator-controlled at 145.249.115[.]184, receives bot registrations containing infection metadata and reachability info.

- Commands appear to originate from an IP belonging to Google's stun.l[.]google[.]com service. Nozomi's analysis points to source-address spoofing through a network provider that does not validate source addresses. TTL differences between genuine STUN replies and command-bearing packets are one of the few network-level tells that something is wrong.

- Observed commands included internet-wide scanning for additional vulnerable targets, TCP tunneling, proxying, and UDP/TCP flood attacks. Confirmed DDoS targets included a South Korean 🇰🇷 ISP, a University of Chicago cluster, and two Minecraft servers.

- Host artifacts are concrete and huntable: malware copies named .cling, persistence entries written to init scripts, and a replaced wget binary with companion files named wget.r and wget.p. Because most compromised devices offer no EDR telemetry, these filesystem indicators and network-layer patterns are often the only evidence available.

Detection priority: at the network layer, hunt for STUN Binding Requests sent at short, regular intervals with transaction IDs set to all zeros, and for non-STUN UDP datagrams directed at known STUN endpoints. At the host layer, scan internet-facing embedded devices for files named .cling, modified init scripts, and replaced wget binaries. Reputation alone cannot be trusted here as packets sourced from high-reputation infrastructure are exactly what the operator is manufacturing. The full IOC list and ATT&CK mapping are in the Nozomi Networks Labs report.

item.title: ClickFix Smuggles Payloads Through Browser Cache to Bypass Windows Run Limits
item.description:
ClickFix evolves: browser cache smuggling hides VBScript payloads from Windows Run dialog limits, bypassing character restrictions while credential-stealing .NET assemblies inject into timeout.exe.
Key findings:
- The attack chain begins on a compromised website that pre-fetches a VBScript payload disguised as a PNG file into the browser cache, typically under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles. When the victim pastes the short ClickFix command into the Windows Run dialog, it executes locally cached content rather than pulling from a remote server, bypassing the roughly 260-character truncation limit and reducing the network footprint that defenders would normally see. The staged script is identified by byte-length comparison across files prefixed "f_", then copied to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp\t.vbs and launched via wscript.exe with output suppressed.
- From t.vbs, cmd.exe enumerates the cache, wscript.exe executes the payload, and WMI harvests host information. A PowerShell script (v.ps1) is then fetched from cocojambo[.]us[.]com/alfa, which delivers an intermediate PowerShell stage responsible for downloading cab.dat. That file's contents are read and executed in a hidden window, loading .NET assemblies in memory that inject code into a freshly spawned timeout.exe, targeting browser and device credentials. The injected process reaches back to capsysnet[.]vg for a secondary in-memory stage and initiates outbound connections to ciliabula[.]cc.
- Nation-state actors are actively adopting this technique. North Korean 🇰🇵 cluster Stardust Chollima (BlueNoroff) was observed in July 2026 using a fake video conferencing site to deliver a PowerShell and VBScript chain introducing two new malware families: GeniexLoader and GeniexRAT. Russian 🇷🇺 state-sponsored Sandworm has been observed targeting suspected Ukrainian 🇺🇦 employees at organizations in France 🇫🇷, the US 🇺🇸, and Canada 🇨🇦 with ClickFix lures delivered via compromised Ukrainian 🇺🇦 websites, using PowerShell commands that download a VBScript payload.
- Infrastructure rotation is being handled via blockchain using the EtherHiding technique, meaning attackers update active lure hostnames on-chain without touching the compromised site. CTM360 identified more than 3,000 actively compromised websites serving fake pages, with attack chains leading to Vidar Stealer. CVE-2026-6854, a vulnerability in WordPress plugins, is being exploited for initial site compromise to inject the ClickFix lures. Fake CAPTCHA lures specifically have seen a 563% increase in 2025 per CrowdStrike.
- The DFIR artifact priority here is clear: RunMRU registry key (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU) captures what the victim pasted into the Run dialog, giving you the exact command and a timestamp anchor. From there, trace wscript.exe and PowerShell child process trees in Security and Sysmon event logs, look for t.vbs in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp, examine the browser cache profile directories for PNG-disguised scripts with byte lengths inconsistent with image data, and check for timeout.exe spawned outside its normal context as the injection host.
Hunt priority: enable PowerShell script-block logging if not already active, it will capture v.ps1 content on execution. Correlate RunMRU entries with wscript.exe or cmd.exe process creation events timestamped within seconds. IOCs including cocojambo[.]us[.]com/alfa, capsysnet[.]vg, and ciliabula[.]cc are named in Microsoft's report alongside detection guidance covering suspicious browser activity, WScript/PowerShell child processes, and scheduled tasks.

item.title: New Stealthy Linux Backdoors Target Telecoms, Masquerade as Email Traffic
item.description:
China-nexus operators deploy stealthy Linux backdoors against South Korean 🇰🇷 and Taiwanese 🇹🇼 telecoms, hiding C2 inside SMTP traffic and masquerading as legitimate mail and anti-spam services on the very devices where that traffic belongs.
Key findings:
- Rapid7 tracked three distinct implant families in this campaign. BPFDoor and BPF Rekoobe variants hit South Korean 🇰🇷 targets, with both naming their processes after SpamSniper, a legitimate South Korean 🇰🇷 anti-spam product, while a separate BPFDoor sample posed as processes on Oracle-based telecom subscriber platforms. Six builds of a new implant called AVERAT were deployed against Taiwanese 🇹🇼 appliances. A BPFDoor controller wraps its trigger packets inside HTTPS POST requests, a technique Rapid7 says can survive edge proxies and bypass conventional deep-packet inspection.
- AVERAT's tradecraft on mail security gateways is the standout finding. The implant beacons outbound on TCP port 25, speaks SMTP, issues an EHLO handshake, and requests STARTTLS before pivoting to its own encrypted session. On a mail gateway whose entire job is handling outbound SMTP, that traffic is invisible in flow records. AVERAT checks in every 600 to 699 seconds and supports file transfers, process termination, up to ten concurrent shell sessions, and proxy or port-forwarding channels.
- The BPF Rekoobe sample triggers only on packets where both source and destination ports are 25, meaning a normal firewall rule permitting mail relay between servers would pass the trigger packet before any stateful inspection engine sees it. This is a deliberate abuse of the trust model that mail infrastructure operators have built around port 25.
- Three AVERAT builds report to hardcoded C2 addresses on compromised third-party devices in Taiwan 🇹🇼: a Synology NAS, an obsolete small-business appliance, and a Dahua video recorder. All three ran an identical PPTP VPN service Rapid7 believes the operators installed to create persistent relay routes. This infrastructure matches the operational relay box (ORB) network profile described in CISA's April 2026 advisory on China-nexus covert networks. Rapid7 found no overlap with any named ORB network and says attribution is ongoing.
- Detection opportunities are specific. Rapid7 flags unexpected raw packet sockets and BPF filters on edge appliances as the clearest host-based signal. On the network side, hunt outbound port 25 connections originating from processes that are not mail transfer agents. On Linux hosts, inspect running process names against the device's expected service list: processes impersonating SpamSniper components or common daemons on hardware that should not run those services are a direct indicator. Restricting management access to routers, DVRs, and edge appliances removes the initial foothold surface for relay node compromise.
Practitioner takeaway: On any Linux edge appliance in scope, pull the list of raw sockets (check /proc/net/raw and /proc/net/raw6) and dump active BPF filters with tc filter show. Cross-reference running process names against the device's known-good service baseline. Alert on any non-MTA process holding an established outbound connection to port 25. Full IOC list and build details are in the Rapid7 report.

item.title: Realtek Jungle SDK Exploit Attempts Deliver Cling Botnet With STUN-Based C2
item.description:
Cling botnet exploits CVE-2021-35394 (CVSS 9.8) in Realtek Jungle SDK, abusing public STUN infrastructure to disguise C2 traffic as legitimate NAT-traversal activity across routers, DVRs, and embedded Linux devices.
Key details:
- Exploitation of CVE-2021-35394 spiked around September 5, 2026, delivering Cling (also tracked as ClingSTUN by Fortinet). The botnet embeds hard-coded exploits for seven CVEs used in self-propagation: CVE-2014-8361 (Realtek), CVE-2016-20016 (MVPower), CVE-2023-26801 (LB-LINK), CVE-2023-41011 (China 🇨🇳 Mobile/FiberHome), CVE-2024-3721 (TBK DVR), CVE-2025-34037 (Linksys), and CVE-2026-87827 (KGUARD DVR). Initial access spans a much wider set including D-Link, Tenda, Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887), TP-Link CVE-2023-1389, AVTECH CVE-2024-7029, and others.
- The C2 mechanism is the standout: Cling sends STUN Binding Requests to 13 hard-coded servers every five seconds, using an all-zero transaction ID (a deliberate protocol deviation). It then sends custom UDP registration datagrams containing mapped ports and infection-source tags like realtek.selfrep or selfrep.router. Operator commands arrive embedded in the STUN transaction ID field. The controlled server 145.249.115[.]184 returns all-zero transaction IDs rather than echoing the request, the tell that it is operator-controlled. More striking: observed command packets originate from 74.125.250[.]129, an IP resolving to stun.l[.]google[.]com, making malicious replies visually indistinguishable from Google STUN responses.
- Persistence is layered: the binary copies itself to /root/.cling and /usr/local/bin/.cling, then appends both paths to /etc/inittab, /etc/init.d/rcS, and /etc/rc.d/rc.boot for SysV and BusyBox init survival. A secondary persistence method replaces the legitimate wget binary with the malware, relocating the original, so any legitimate process invoking wget executes the bot instead. Single-instance enforcement uses SO_REUSEADDR on port 33957.
- Once established, Cling supports recursive scanning and worm-like spread, TCP tunnel spawn/stop, proxy launch/stop, and timed DoS floods. Observed flood targets include 112.151.157[.]222:8080, 192.170.240[.]137:53, and Minecraft servers at 23.81.40[.]193:25565 and 147.185.221[.]129:25565. Payloads are fetched via shell script downloaders for ARM, MIPS R3000, PowerPC, Intel 80386, and AMD X86-64, maximizing the range of vulnerable embedded hardware.
Network defenders: hunt outbound UDP to port 3478 with zero-byte transaction IDs and flag UDP datagrams to public STUN servers that do not conform to RFC 5389 (non-random transaction IDs, oversized or non-standard payloads). On the host side, check for /root/.cling, /usr/local/bin/.cling, and modifications to /etc/inittab or rcS. Validate the wget binary hash against a known-good baseline: a replaced wget is a clean persistence indicator with no legitimate use case. Port 33957 bound with SO_REUSEADDR on a router or DVR is a direct Cling presence signal. Full IOC list is in the Nozomi Networks report.

item.title: How Huntress Detects and Responds to a ClickFix Attack
item.description:
ClickFix beats most endpoint tools by design, not sophistication. The delivery mechanism is a user, a Run dialog, and a paste, and that leaves nothing for artifact-based controls to catch.
Key findings:
- The structural gap is architectural, not a tuning problem. Signature AV, NGAV, and most EDR are built around an artifact arriving: a file to hash, scan, or quarantine. ClickFix skips that entirely. The user is the dropper. From the endpoint's perspective, a person launching a program is the most ordinary event of their day. Backend telemetry detections do fire, but ClickFix chains complete in seconds, so by the time an alert surfaces and an analyst picks it up, the infostealer has already run and credentials are already gone. Detection and stopping are two different outcomes.
- A real incident shows exactly how layered the evasion is. The attacker's verbatim command pasted into the Run dialog stacked three bypass techniques in one line: caret escaping (s^t^a^r^t, f^^i^^n^^g^^e^^r) to defeat string matching, padding that scrolled the real command out of the dialog's visible field leaving only "P_u_s_h t_h_e En_t_e_r k_e_y" visible to the victim, and finger.exe as the download cradle. finger.exe is a signed Windows binary shipping since 1991. It fetched the payload as a plain text string over the finger protocol. No curl, no PowerShell, no file on disk, no unsigned binary. The C2 domain in the defanged command was finger.linkeders[.]net. The user pasted the same command six times between 18:07 and 18:53, each attempt killed on arrival.
- The detection chokepoint is the parent-child relationship, not the payload. When a user runs something via the Run dialog, the parent is always explorer.exe. Always. An obfuscated download cradle on its own is debatable signal. An obfuscated download cradle spawned directly by explorer.exe in an interactive session has no innocent explanation. That parent gate is what makes aggressive automated termination safe enough to leave on. The four-process chain in the incident was spawned and fully terminated in 1.25 seconds: cmd.exe lived 620ms, a detached shell lived 625ms, a subshell lived 465ms, finger.exe lived 397ms. The loop body that would have executed the returned payload never ran because the shell it needed was dead 11ms before finger.exe exited.
- A critical gap was found and closed during development. Some ClickFix variants use start to detach the follow-on process, orphaning it from the parent before termination. The fix was a second rule matching on the parent's command line and killing both parent and child simultaneously, which also neutralizes randomly renamed launchers. Coverage has since expanded to homoglyph and Unicode abuse, scheme-less URIs, comment-block command construction, and a broader LOLBIN surface. The ruleset moved from a handful of broad rules to a larger set of narrowly scoped sub-detections.
- Enforce mode is the only mode that matters here. A control that warns is one the socially engineered user clicks past. The sixth paste attempt must be as dead as the first. The report is explicit that this is disruption, not prevention, Windows-specific in this implementation, and not total coverage: attackers rotate LOLBINs and obfuscation, and new variants (FileFix, TerminalFix, DownloadFix) require new pattern work. When the agent-side kill loses the race, backend detections still produce an investigation, just not a termination.
Hunt focus: query process creation logs for cmd.exe or PowerShell spawned directly by explorer.exe in interactive sessions (logon type 2) containing IEX, IRM, finger, or heavy caret usage in the command line. That parent-child pair with an obfuscated command line is the structural tell that holds across variants. The report includes a full technical breakdown of ClickFix, FileFix, TerminalFix, and DownloadFix with host artifacts and detection chokepoints for each variant.
